text.p: Croatia presented a 39.4 billion kuna 1997 budget proposal on Friday, up around 10 percent from this year's spending and designed to spur economic recovery as well as boost welfare programmes.
Officials said borrowing would increase despite higher revenues but this would not endanger the deficit target of under three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
"The central government deficit will be 2.63 percent of GDP," Deputy Prime Minister Borislav Skegro told a news conference.
He said nominal GDP was projected to rise some nine percent to 108 billion kuna next year.
Skegro said the central government would further trim its spending in order to inject money into the ailing industrial and public sectors without widening the external debt too much.
"We are trying to save as a state in order to reinvest. The contrary, borrowing abroad to cover current expenditures, would be perilous and we could not to it anyway," Skegro said.
Croatia plans to issue Eurobonds in 1997 and also raise a sizeable amount from official creditors and banks to finance reconstruction and development plans.

But it will have to repay four billion kuna in matured old debt, including firt portions of the rescheduled liabilities to the so-called Paris Club of government lenders and foreign commercial creditors of the London Club.
According to the budget draft made available to reporters, public spending will increase to 35.5 billion kuna from 33.3 billion budgeted this year.

Finance Minister Bozo Prka said the budget could be termed a "development and social budget'. While counting on higher revenues of 32.7 billion, up by five percent from 1996, Prka said the government had also built into the budget some tax cuts to relieve the economy and improve the fragile social structure.
He said taxpayers would not be directly affected by higher tax revenues as they would be supported by continued growth.
On top of some 4.3 billion kuna capital investments, government would increase payouts to ailing industrial branches such as shipbuilding and textiles, and the banking sector.
The banking sector will get an injection of 820 million kuna to complete its overhaul, Prka said.
Social transfers and subsidies, partly to increase payouts to help the worst-off citizens such as war invalids and pensioners, would total over eight billion kuna.
Prka said the government aimed to keep its promise to raise workers wages next year after keeping a lid on pay rises since 1993 in a drive to stabilise the economy.
